The tide-cell smells of kelp and old iron, and the water is at his ankles when I come down the steps. I like it at this hour. The sea is honest about what it wants.

Desmond Kai is chained to the wall by one wrist, the left, which leaves the right free. I asked for that. A poet should keep the hand he works with, until he doesn't.

"Magistra," he says. His voice is wrecked from shouting at the gulls through the grate. "If you've come for a reading, I charge double for tyrants."

I laugh, and I mean it. That is the trouble with Desmond; he is good company. I sit on the dry step Hobb has swept for me and fold my hands in my lap.

"Your pamphlets reached the fish market again," I tell him. "Someone glued one to my barge. Rhymed couplets, Desmond. About my teeth."

"They were accurate couplets."

"They were." I nod to Hobb. Hobb is the size of a door and has a burn across his scalp that never grew back hair; it shines like a peeled egg in the lamplight. He wades in and takes Desmond's right hand in both of his, gently, the way a man holds a bird.

"The first finger," I say, "is for the couplets."

Hobb bends the index finger back against the knuckle until it cracks. It is a wet, short sound, like a green stick under a boot, and the finger sits wrong after that, pointing at the ceiling. Desmond screams. I watch his mouth, not his hand. The mouth is where the poetry was.

"I enjoy this," I tell him, when he can hear me again. "Not the noise. The arithmetic. You spent years making my people laugh at me, and it will take you a month to hold a spoon."

He spits. It lands short.

"The second," I say, "is for the fish market."

Hobb takes the middle finger. This one does not crack; it gives way at the middle joint with a sound like a knot pulled through wet rope, and the skin over it whitens and splits. Desmond's knees go, and the chain catches him, and the sea slaps at his thighs. Hobb waits, patient as a bell-ringer.

"You'll write with the left," Desmond says, through his teeth. "Badly. It'll improve the verse."

That one is good. I will repeat it at dinner and claim it.

"The third," I say, "is because I came all the way down here."

Hobb breaks the ring finger at the base, quickly, almost kindly, and the snap of it is the cleanest of the three. I hear it over the water. I keep my eyes on Desmond's face the whole time, because a ruler who flinches is a ruler who can be pushed, and I am not that.

The tide is turning. In an hour it will be at his chest. Hobb wipes his palms on his apron and climbs out, and I stand and shake the damp from my hem.

Desmond is crying now, quietly, without shame. I admire that, too.

"Write me something about the water," I tell him, from the top step. "You have until it reaches your mouth."
